source.title: Evaluasi Optimizer Adam dan RMSProp pada Arsitektur VGG-19 Klasifikasi Ekspresi Wajah Manusia

record.tranche_reason: The study compares batch-size settings and reports training and validation accuracy for each, testing batch-size effects on the held-out performance gap with a different task and model than the cited large-batch studies.
record.gate_note: The batch-size and epoch sweeps report training accuracy, validation accuracy, and loss in Tables IV–V. The paper also reports test-set classification metrics for the selected Adam and RMSProp models. It does not test the other claim versions.
record.test_reason: Tables IV–V test V5 in a new image-classification setting: modified VGG-19 on FER2013, varying batch size within fixed 25- or 50-epoch budgets. Adam versus RMSProp does not test V4 because neither comparator is SGD.
record.authors_conclusion: The record correctly identifies the authors' preference for Adam and their selected configurations. However, the stated 91.26% and 84.60% figures are validation-to-training accuracy ratios, calculated from R4 and R13, rather than held-out accuracies. The conclusion misleadingly calls them accuracies. The evaluation discussion reports overall accuracy around 66% for both optimizers, so the claimed Adam advantage is not established by those ratios.
record.recipe_differences: Compares two adaptive optimizers on VGG-19 for facial-expression classification; does not use the optimizer comparisons or benchmarks specified in the claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported validation results vary with batch size and epoch; Adam and RMSProp have different selected settings.

fits_no_version.finding: The authors prefer Adam over RMSProp using selected configurations with different batch sizes and epoch counts.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Relative performance of two adaptive optimizers on FER2013 under separately selected training configurations.

record.peer_reviewed: JIPI (Jurnal Ilmiah Penelitian dan Pembelajaran Informatika), Vol. 10, No. 2, 2025
record.problems: No repeated runs or uncertainty estimates are reported. The reported test evaluation is limited to selected configurations, and selected Adam and RMSProp settings differ in batch size and epoch count. The abstract and conclusion give accuracy values of 91.26% and 84.60%, while the test-set evaluation tables report overall accuracy around 0.64 and 0.66; the text does not resolve this discrepancy. Table IV–V accuracy column units are not stated.

untested.parts: No random-label training or natural-label versus random-label comparison.
No width sweep or interpolation-threshold measurement.
No fully connected comparator or connectivity intervention.
No SGD comparator, broader optimizer tuning comparison, decoupled weight decay, or Adam-to-SGD switch.

No language models, learning-rate scaling, warmup, or normalization/regularization interventions. The two epoch budgets do not establish a converged large-batch threshold or whether longer training closes a penalty relative to a fixed small-batch target.
Dropout is present but neither varied nor ablated.
No weight-perturbation sharpness measurements or comparison of generalization measures.
No identification or removal of memorized examples.

record.verdict_notes: All table values match the supplied text. Accuracy values are interpretable as percentages. Loss is described in the surrounding prose as validation loss. Row states use the explicitly named within-optimizer, fixed-epoch baselines; reference rows cannot establish an effect alone. V5 allows a workload-dependent threshold, so improved accuracy when increasing batch size from 32 does not itself challenge V5 or require monotonic deterioration across the entire sweep. No repeated runs or uncertainty estimates are given, and the validation split is not clearly described.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label training or comparison of random-label and natural-label generalization.
No width sweep or interpolation-threshold analysis.
No fully connected comparator or local-connectivity intervention.
Compares Adam with RMSProp, not adaptive optimizers with SGD or momentum SGD; no broader tuning, decoupled weight decay, or optimizer switch.

Tests batch sizes 32, 64, 128, and 256 at 25 or 50 epochs on FER2013 using VGG-19 and Adam or RMSProp. Does not test language models, workload-dependent thresholding, longer training beyond 50 epochs, or recipe adaptations such as learning-rate scaling with warmup. The best Adam and RMSProp settings differ in both batch size and epoch count.
Dropout is included in the modified architecture but is not ablated or varied.
No memorized-example identification, removal, or retraining comparison.

relationships.reason: R6–R8 show nearly equal accuracy at batches 64 and 128 and only a 0.8638-point decline at 256; the upper-range penalty is much smaller than at 25 epochs.
relationships.display_finding: Validation accuracy was nearly equal at batches 64 and 128 before declining by 0.8638 points at batch 256. This batch-size penalty was smaller than the corresponding batch-size penalty after 25 epochs of training.

relation.reason: Tables IV–V directly bear on V5 through validation accuracy across batch sizes at shared epoch budgets. Adam versus RMSProp does not test V4's adaptive-versus-SGD comparison.

tranche.reason: Modified VGG-19 on FER2013 supplies a new image-classification setting with batch-size comparisons under fixed 25- and 50-epoch budgets.

source_check.notes: Tables IV–V provide validation comparisons without repeated-run uncertainty. The abstract's 91.26% and 84.60% are validation-to-training accuracy ratios; the conclusion misleadingly calls them accuracies.

statements.correction: Table IV: Adam, learning rate 0.0001; validation accuracy at batches 64/128/256 = 67.1628/65.5196/61.1452 at 25 epochs and 65.8326/65.8958/65.0320 at 50 epochs; no repeated-run uncertainty reported; 50-epoch pattern supports limits_scope.
statements.problem: The numbers and descriptive reversal match Table IV, but the challenges label overstates this study's evidence against V5: the workload-dependent threshold is not established, and batch 256 still performs worse than batches 64 and 128.
